content: Among adolescents, surveillance data indicates that 9% of those with acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection either (a) have had sexual contact with a chronically infected individual or with multiple sexual partners, or (b) identify their sexual preference as homosexual. To eliminate HBV transmission in the United States, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends that all children receive the hepatitis B vaccine. Adolescents at high risk for sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) include male homosexuals, sexually active heterosexuals, clients of STD clinics, and individuals who use injection drugs. Adolescents under the age of 15 who are sexually active are particularly vulnerable to infection. Adolescents are at the greatest risk for STDs due to frequent engagement in unprotected sexual intercourse, increased biological susceptibility to infections, and various barriers to accessing healthcare services. Clinicians who provide care to adolescents can address these issues by improving knowledge and awareness about the risks and consequences of STDs. They can also offer guidance to promote healthy sexual behaviors and prevent the establishment of patterns that may compromise sexual health. In the United States, with limited exceptions, adolescents can consent to confidential STD diagnosis and treatment without requiring parental consent or knowledge. In many states, adolescents can also consent to HIV counseling and testing. Consent laws for adolescent vaccination vary by state, with some states allowing vaccination services without parental consent, treating them similarly to STD treatment. Providers should recognize the importance of confidentiality for adolescents and adhere to state laws to ensure the privacy of STD-related services. Counseling and health education for adolescents should be tailored to their developmental level and should address risky behaviors, such as sexual activity and drug use. Careful, nonjudgmental counseling is particularly important for adolescents who may not acknowledge engaging in high-risk behaviors. Management of children with STDs requires close collaboration between clinicians, laboratory personnel, and child protection authorities. Investigations, when warranted, should be initiated promptly. Certain STDs, such as gonorrhea, syphilis, and chlamydia, if acquired after the neonatal period, are almost always indicative of sexual contact. For other conditions, such as HPV infection and vaginitis, the association with sexual contact is less clear. HIV infection progresses through a spectrum of disease, ranging from a clinically latent or asymptomatic state to AIDS as the late manifestation. The rate of disease progression varies, with the time from HIV infection to AIDS development ranging from a few months to as long as 17 years (median: 10 years). Most adults and adolescents with HIV remain asymptomatic for extended periods, but active viral replication occurs throughout all stages of infection, increasing significantly as the immune system deteriorates. AIDS eventually develops in nearly all HIV-infected individuals. In one study, 87% of HIV-infected adults developed AIDS within 17 years of infection, with additional cases expected among those who remain AIDS-free for longer periods. Increased awareness of HIV transmission risk factors among patients and healthcare providers has led to more frequent HIV testing and earlier diagnosis, often before symptoms appear. Early diagnosis of HIV infection is critical for several reasons. Treatments are available to slow the decline of immune system function and to prevent opportunistic infections, such as Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia, toxoplasmic encephalitis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex disease, tuberculosis, and bacterial pneumonia. HIV also affects the diagnosis, evaluation, treatment, and follow-up of other diseases and may influence the efficacy of antimicrobial therapy for some STDs. Early diagnosis of HIV enables healthcare providers to counsel patients and assist in preventing HIV transmission to others. Proper management of HIV infection requires a comprehensive array of behavioral, psychosocial, and medical services. While some of these services may be available in STD treatment facilities, others, particularly medical services, are often unavailable in such settings. Referral to a healthcare provider or facility experienced in managing HIV-infected patients is recommended. Staff in STD treatment facilities should be knowledgeable about referral options available in their communities. While in the STD treatment facility, HIV-infected patients should be educated about HIV infection and the various care options available. Due to the complexity of services required for managing HIV infection, detailed information, particularly regarding medical care, is beyond the scope of this report and can be found in other sources.
